items.summary: Kevin Warsh enters Day 11 as Federal Reserve Chair without a single public statement — the deepest communication vacuum of any modern Fed chair transition in the inflation-targeting era, now extending into its third week. The Brent crude Monday open at $102-103 represents a structural new input that the Fed cannot ignore: for the first time since the conflict began, a plausible near-term disinflationary pathway has received market confirmation. The April 2026 CPI print stands at 3.8% year-on-year — the highest since May 2023 — with energy costs up 17.9% annually, the steepest energy increase since September 2022; gasoline specifically up 28.4% and fuel oil up 54.3%. Core CPI edged to 2.8% YoY, the highest since September. PPI runs at 6.0% annualized. These readings are exclusively upstream of the April 29 WPA statutory deadline and do not yet reflect any deal-driven energy price moderation — the April data is the pre-deal baseline against which any future crude-driven disinflation will be measured. The Brent Monday open ($102-103 vs. $105-107) is the first data point suggesting a potential path below that baseline. However, quantification is difficult: even a confirmed deal announcement this week would require weeks of Hormuz transit normalization before retail energy prices respond. The $3-4 Brent decline translates to approximately $0.07-0.10 per gallon at the pump over a 4-6 week lag — meaningful at the margin, not transformational. Warsh's silence means the Fed has provided no anchor for interpreting the deal signal, the April CPI print, or the Treasury yield complex. The 10-year held near 4.57% Friday; the 30-year held near 5.07% (intraweek high 5.19%, the highest since 2007). Foreign holders — Saudi Arabia, Japan — continue trimming US Treasuries. The December 2026 rate hike probability stands near 40% as of the latest CME filing. June FOMC is 23 days out with approximately 98% hold probability for the June meeting itself. Warsh's first communication, whenever it arrives, must now contend with a new variable: an energy market actively pricing deal probability. If the deal is confirmed and Brent moves materially lower, the disinflationary pathway materially changes the rate trajectory — but Warsh's silence means the Fed has no public position on that pathway. The communication gap is compounding, not stabilizing.

items.summary: The Iran war advances to Day 26 past the April 29 WPA statutory deadline and to four days before the May 29 90-day hard deadline. Congress returns tomorrow, May 26 — creating a three-calendar-day window (May 26, 27, 28) before the most consequential legal milestone of the current conflict cycle. Trump's 'largely negotiated' deal declaration does not reset the WPA clock under any reading of the statute: a presidential announcement of a 'largely negotiated' deal is not cessation of hostilities; cessation requires the Hormuz strait to reopen, the naval blockade to be lifted, and the physical end of conflict-related military operations. With Brent at $102-103 and Hormuz physically closed, the preconditions for cessation of hostilities are not met as of Monday morning. Even if a formal deal text were confirmed today, implementation of Hormuz reopening and blockade lifting would require days to weeks of transit normalization negotiation — the physical WPA threshold will not be crossed by May 29 regardless of any announcement. House Republican leadership has explicitly scheduled its next war powers vote for early June — after the deadline. The Senate has no 8th war powers resolution scheduled. The bipartisan House majority coalition (Rep. Golden confirmed yes, six Republicans voting with Democrats) is real but dormant. The administration's 'hostilities terminated' posture — asserting the ceasefire pause stopped the WPA clock — does not survive Day 90 plain-text scrutiny: Hormuz is closed, the naval blockade is active, and the pause is executive discretion, not statutory cessation. At Day 90 on May 29, the Iran war will operate definitionally beyond any credible statutory basis under any operative legal theory. Any administration legal statement on this architecture in light of the deal announcement would be a priority watch signal for May 26-28. The first congressional opportunity to address the changed legal architecture arrives in early June — after the threshold has already been crossed.

The downstream effects on Oregon and Washington agricultural workforce availability entering fire and harvest season deserve near-term monitoring. Second: Secretary Rubio is in New Delhi for Quad ministerial consultations — covered in geopolitical section; the domestic angle is the signal that the administration views Indo-Pacific alliance maintenance as a parallel priority during the Iran conflict cycle, with implications for defense spending and supplemental authorization trajectories. Third: Kevin Warsh is Day 11 without a public statement. The Brent crude Monday open ($102-103) is the first material new economic signal of his Fed chairmanship — a disinflationary input he will eventually need to address publicly. June FOMC is 23 days out. Any Warsh communication is the highest-priority domestic economic signal of the current cycle; none is scheduled. Fourth: the national measles count stood at 1,952 confirmed cases as of May 21, up 59 from the 1,893 on May 14, averaging approximately 8.4 cases per day. Oregon Health Authority measles data is 33 days stale — last published 20 confirmed cases on April 22 with no update despite the May 12 first Oregon hospitalization (discharged, recovering), ongoing Washington State outbreak activity (40+ cases, 8 counties, Kittitas County active), and the accelerating national count. The school vaccination window is approximately 3-4 operative days — Memorial Day removed Monday from the coordination calendar; the last organized school-based intervention opportunity is effectively closing. Community health and outpatient settings are already the de facto primary intervention channels. Any new county outbreak declaration, second Oregon hospitalization, or school-exposure event in the next 3-4 days constitutes a critical escalation with the window closing.

items.headline: OHA Measles 33 Days Stale — National 1,952 (May 21, +59); School Window ~3-4 Operative Days; OR Gas $5.35 / WA $5.78 Memorial Day Record; Green Card Reversal Impacts PNW Agriculture; Portland $172M Shortfall
items.summary: Four PNW threads. First: Oregon Health Authority measles data is 33 days stale — last published count 20 cases on April 22, no update for over a month despite the accelerating national count (1,952 as of May 21, pace ~8.4/day), Washington State active outbreak (40+ cases, 8 counties, Kittitas County active), and the May 12 first Oregon hospitalization (discharged, recovering). The school vaccination window has now contracted to approximately 3-4 operative coordination days with Memorial Day having consumed Monday. The organized school-based campaign is effectively in its final days; community health and outpatient settings are already the de facto primary intervention channels. A new county outbreak declaration, second Oregon hospitalization, or documented school-exposure event in the next 3-4 days constitutes a critical escalation with the window nearly closed. Second: Oregon gasoline holds at $5.35 per gallon Memorial Day Monday — record 2026 high, fourth-highest in the nation. Washington State remains at approximately $5.78 per gallon. National average is $4.56, record 2026 high. Brent's Monday open at $102-103 is the first signal of a potential future pump-relief trajectory, but retail relief requires weeks minimum from confirmed deal plus transit normalization plus supply-chain response. Memorial Day driving demand is occurring at peak fuel cost with approximately 500,000 Oregonians on the road. Third: the Trump administration's Friday green card policy reversal — requiring foreign nationals to leave the US and apply from their home country — has direct implications for PNW agricultural labor supply entering fire and harvest season (late June through September) and for tech-sector workforce stability in the Portland and Seattle metros. The downstream labor supply disruption for Oregon and Washington agriculture deserves monitoring as fire season onset approaches simultaneously. Fourth: Portland's $172 million budget shortfall continues to deepen under record fuel costs, 30-year Treasury above 5%, and state revenue compression from the supply-shock slowdown. Council action will be required post-recess.

analyst_summary: Memorial Day Monday, May 25, 2026 — Hormuz Day 87, Naval Blockade Day 44, Project Freedom Pause Day 20, WPA Day 26 Past Statutory Deadline / 4 Days to 90-Day Hard Deadline May 29, Warsh Day 11. Vibe 4. The defining development of the overnight cycle is Brent crude's Monday open at approximately $102-103 per barrel — down $3-4 from the $105-107 range that held through the Saturday evening filing. This is the first quantitative market-credibility signal for Trump's 'largely negotiated' declaration: energy traders have priced conditional belief. The Brent signal is meaningful — it implies roughly 55-65% deal probability in current market consensus — but it is not conviction. Full conviction would yield a $15-20+ decline toward the pre-conflict baseline of $75-85; $3-4 is the market's conditional hedge. The structural state of the deal itself is unchanged from Saturday evening: Trump publicly committed + full regional coalition consulted + Iran FM 'framework agreement' language = strongest positive signal of the cycle; Iran Fars dismissal + no Mojtaba Khamenei statement + no FM formal text confirmation = signal unconfirmed. The vibe holds at 4. The WPA 90-day hard deadline is 4 days away. Federal channels are closed through today — Memorial Day. Congress returns tomorrow, May 26 — 3 calendar days before the legal architecture changes at Day 90 on May 29. House war powers next attempt: early June, explicitly after the deadline. Senate: no 8th resolution. Any deal announcement does not reset the WPA clock; the Hormuz strait will not be physically open by May 29 regardless of any text confirmed before then. Warsh Day 11 extends the deepest Fed communication gap of the modern inflation-targeting era: the Brent Monday open is the first material disinflationary input of his chairmanship, and the Fed has no public position on it. April CPI at 3.8% YoY (highest since May 2023), energy +17.9%, Core 2.8% — the pre-deal baseline against which any crude-driven relief will be measured. Oregon fire season is Day 18 with 7 days to east Cascades above-normal onset; Stage 1 Central Oregon active; 82% statewide drought; Southern Cascades extreme; prepositioning window 7 days; delegation letter 18 days unanswered; tomorrow is the first federal legislative response opportunity. OHA measles data is 33 days stale; national at 1,952 (May 21); school window at ~3-4 operative days — effectively closing. Green card policy reversal announced Friday adds a new PNW labor-supply uncertainty vector entering fire and harvest season. Oregon gas at $5.35, national at $4.56 — record 2026 Memorial Day highs with half a million Oregonians on the road. The Brent signal is the morning's analytical anchor. Vibe 4.
